chapter: Writing, Oklahoma roots and the origins of bebop
title: Fletcher Henderson, the Grand Terrace and radio
summary: He listened from Oklahoma to the Grand Terrace broadcasts, then played there with Kirk and found it disappointing.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: How about Don Redman and Fletcher Henderson and that whole thing?
Well, I liked Fletcher's band when he came out West to the Grand Terrace and played "Christopher Columbus" with Chu Berry and Roy...
That was 1936.

Well, I liked that. I used to listen to them from Oklahoma City. I could get Chicago on the radio. So I used to listen to Earl Hines and Fletcher Henderson and all the bands that played in the Grand Terrace. I thought about that when I was in the Grand Terrace. I said, "Gee, I used to be so glad to be..."
[END OF TAPE 3, SIDE 2]
You were saying that you had listened to all the broadcasts from the Grand Terrace when you were out in Oklahoma, and then here you were playing there.
Oh, you mean at the Grand Terrace.
Yes. When did you play there?
With Andy Kirk's band. This was in '41, I think.
And you said to yourself...
McGhee (12/6) - 7

Yeah, I remember me being in Oklahoma and listening to the bands from the Grand Terrace, and here I was working there. Which was all the difference... But it was like a drag being there, you know, thinking about it, because it wasn't what I had pictured it to be. I always had created... I mean, it said The Grand Terrace. I figured everything was grand, and they had a beautiful terrace and all this. The Grand Terrace! I put the words together and tried to figure that out. But when I got to the Grand Terrace, I said, 'This is it? Wow!' What the hell. I mean, but that's the way it was in them days. So I set my foolish dreams aside, and went on and made the gig like I was supposed to. But I heard all of the bands that had come from there, though.
Well, radio was such an important thing.

Yeah. It was the only form of communication that you could hear, especially about music. Like, very seldom did they have a whole lot of bands playing on the radio that was playing something. They had a lot of bands playing music that you'd hear over and over and over, but they didn't have no distinctive bands that you could listen to. You know how it is.
It was harder than hell to hear something fresh. Did you hear anything fresh lately?
McGhee (12/6) - 8
Well, I've heard some fresh things. I don't say I like it, but they're fresh.
[LAUGHS] Yeah. Like what?
That's for another time.
Well, we're all here talking, right?
Yeah, but it's not in keeping with what we're talking about. I want to go back in time.
All right, let's back there, then.
